children: Fears of a U.S. sovereign debt crisis may be overstated because investors are focusing too narrowly on government liabilities while overlooking the enormous private-sector asset base supporting the economy, according to Discipline Funds founder and CIO Cullen Roche.
Roche argued that the nearly $500 trillion in U.S. private-sector assets changes how investors should think about rising federal debt and Treasury yields.
Ignore all the sovereign debt crisis talk, Roche wrote, adding that inflation expectations are adjusting to something more historically normalized.
His argument comes as the 10-year Treasury yield has climbed to about 5.19%, reviving concerns over debt sustainability and the rising cost of financing federal deficits.
Roche says that level looks less alarming in historical context. The 10-year Treasury yield has averaged roughly 5.8% since 1960, meaning current yields remain below the long-term average.
The bigger issue, in his view, is what investors leave out of the balance sheet.

Roche estimates total gross private-sector assets at roughly $489 trillion, around 10 times the size of U.S. public debt. He argues that focusing on sovereign liabilities without considering the tax base and private wealth behind them creates a distorted picture of the country's financial position.
That does not eliminate the risks.

The Council on Foreign Relations has warned that foreign investors may increasingly demand a higher risk premium to hold U.S. debt, potentially weakening the country's long-standing ability to borrow cheaply as issuer of the world's dominant reserve currency.
For bond investors, the disagreement comes down to whether rising Treasury yields reflect a genuine solvency concern or a normalization in inflation and term premiums.
If Roche is right, current yield levels may say more about inflation expectations than an approaching debt crisis.
But the counterargument matters too: even a wealthy economy can face higher financing costs if deficits continue expanding and foreign demand weakens.
Investors should watch the 10-year Treasury yield, foreign Treasury demand, inflation expectations, federal interest expense and the dollar.
The $489 trillion private-sector asset base is a powerful counterweight to the debt-crisis narrative, but it does not make rising borrowing costs irrelevant.

title: Treasury Yield Surge Revives U.S. Debt Crisis Debate
